title: Clarity
tagline: Making brain rot impossible to ignore
description: A system that progressively changes the digital experience as overstimulation rises.

heroMedia.caption: Clarity concept exploring tactile resistance and real-time overstimulation feedback.

introParagraphs: What if your phone could recognize when scrolling stops feeling good — and make that change impossible to ignore?
Instead of relying on another screen-time notification, we designed the interface itself to respond as digital overstimulation increases.

snapshot.challenge: Help people recognize harmful scrolling while it is happening.
snapshot.concept: A system that progressively changes the digital experience as overstimulation rises.

caseStudy.heading: Scrolling is frictionless even when it stops feeling good.
body: People can move from intentional phone use into passive scrolling without a clear moment where the experience feels different.
Traditional screen-time tools usually intervene after time has passed.
caseStudy.subheading: That gave us a different question:
caseStudy.largeQuestion: How might we make digital overstimulation noticeable while it is happening?

caseStudy.caption: Five-second comprehension: showing how frictionless browsing silently turns into overstimulation.
Passive digital consumption quietly fills every unoccupied moment of the day.

caseStudy.heading: Instead of telling you to stop scrolling, we made scrolling itself respond.
body: This is the key conceptual leap of Clarity.
Rather than adding another notification that could be dismissed, we explored interventions embedded directly into the experience.
As overstimulation rises, the interface becomes progressively harder to ignore.

caseStudy.placeholderTitle: LOW (NORMAL SCROLLING) → RISING (SUBTLE INTERVENTION) → HIGH (STRONG INTERVENTION)
caseStudy.caption: First major product visual: mapping the three tiers of progressive intervention.

caseStudy.heading: Making friction something you can feel
caseStudy.subheading: We chose progressive friction over another screen-time warning.
context: Most digital wellbeing interventions ask users to consciously respond to another alert.
But during passive scrolling, dismissing an alert is easy.
decision: We explored making the interaction itself change instead.
As overstimulation rises, Clarity progressively introduces:

decisionPoints.title: Visual Degradation
decisionPoints.body: The interface gradually loses visual intensity.

decisionPoints.title: Audio Grounding
decisionPoints.body: Chaotic audio gives way to calmer grounding feedback.

why: The goal wasn't to suddenly lock someone out.
It was to create a progression: subtle → noticeable → difficult to ignore.
caseStudy.placeholderTitle: CLARITY — PRODUCT EVIDENCE: HAPTIC → VISUAL → AUDIO
caseStudy.caption: Three synchronous interventions: tactile scroll resistance, desaturating content, and ambient harmonic audio.

cards.title: Audio grounding
cards.body: Changes the sensory environment without adding another alert.

caseStudy.heading: Giving an invisible feeling a visible state
caseStudy.subheading: “Brain rot” was fuzzy, so we gave it a visual language.
context: Overstimulation isn't something users can easily see.
That created a communication problem: How do you represent a gradual cognitive state without asking someone to interpret a dashboard full of metrics?

decisionPoints.title: Brain Rot Level
decisionPoints.body: A simple representation of the system's current state.

decisionPoints.title: Neuro
decisionPoints.body: A character whose appearance responds as that state changes.

why: The number provides clarity. The character provides emotion and immediate recognition.
Instead of requiring users to analyze data, the interface communicates: Something is changing.
caseStudy.placeholderTitle: CLARITY — VISUAL STATE: LOW → MEDIUM → HIGH (NEURO & BRAIN ROT LEVEL)
caseStudy.caption: Neuro's facial expression and color warmth evolve alongside the Brain Rot percentage.

cards.title: Neuro
cards.body: Makes that state recognizable at a glance.

caseStudy.heading: Intervening before another scroll begins
caseStudy.subheading: The best intervention might happen before you reopen the app.
context: If Clarity only works once someone is already deep inside the experience, intervention may come too late.
decision: We extended Clarity into surfaces already present in someone's environment: Dynamic Island and Apple Watch.
These surfaces can communicate state without requiring someone to reopen the main app.
tradeoff: The system needs to remain noticeable without becoming another source of interruption itself.
caseStudy.placeholderTitle: CLARITY — ECOSYSTEM COMPOSITION: WATCH ← NEURO / STATE → DYNAMIC ISLAND
caseStudy.caption: Ambient awareness distributed across the user's immediate physical and screen environment.

cards.title: Dynamic Island
cards.body: Lightweight intervention without leaving the current context.

cards.title: Apple Watch
cards.body: Moves awareness away from the screen being overused.

caseStudy.heading: An attention tool shouldn't become another system controlling your attention.
body: Clarity lets users control what information is tracked, delete their data, and step away from the system.

cards.title: Choose what's tracked
cards.body: Granular toggles for behavioral signals and interventions.

cards.title: Delete your data
cards.body: Instant on-device purge with zero cloud retention.

cards.title: Take a break
cards.body: Pause interventions with a single tap whenever needed.

caseStudy.caption: Transparent user controls putting people back in command of their data and attention.

caseStudy.heading: From passive scrolling to conscious interruption.
caseStudy.conclusion: Clarity turns digital wellbeing from something users check afterward into something they can notice while it is happening.

caseStudy.placeholderTitle: CLARITY — COMPLETE PRODUCT FILM & INTERACTION WALKTHROUGH
caseStudy.caption: End-to-end user journey from scrolling friction to conscious recovery.

caseStudy.heading: The concept raised harder questions than the prototype answered.
body: Clarity was built as a hackathon concept, which meant we could explore an ambitious interaction quickly—but many of its assumptions still need validation and honest critique.

items.heading: Can something as subjective as “brain rot” be represented as a score?
items.body: The concept depends on translating a fuzzy cognitive experience into something legible. I'd want to test whether that representation feels useful or overly reductive.

items.heading: When does helpful friction become annoying?
items.body: The intervention has to interrupt automatic behavior without making ordinary phone use frustrating.

items.heading: Can an intervention reduce distraction without becoming another distraction itself?
items.body: Especially across the Watch and Dynamic Island, the next step would be understanding when intervention helps—and when silence is better.
